title: EASA's AI Olympics Closed Early — and That's Actually the Point
summary: EASA hit its 50-entry cap for its AI Olympics showcase before the July 9 deadline, signaling real industry momentum — but the harder question is whether any of those systems will survive contact with certification.
body_markdown:
The entry window for EASA's inaugural AI Olympics closed on July 7 — two days ahead of the official deadline — because the agency hit its self-imposed cap of 50 submissions. <cite index="32-6,32-7">EASA announced it was no longer accepting entries as the maximum permissible number of 50 had been received, and thanked all entrants while proceeding with evaluation.</cite> The top ten will earn a stage at <cite index="31-1">the 4th edition of EASA AI Days, hosted at EASA's premises in Cologne on September 9–10, 2026.</cite>

That's a small logistical detail that carries a larger signal: the industry has more aviation AI to show than EASA has bandwidth to review.

I think that gap — between the volume of AI being built for aviation and the institutional capacity to evaluate, validate, and eventually certify it — is the most important tension in flight operations technology right now. Not the algorithms. Not the data. The evaluation infrastructure.

## The Showcase Problem

The AI Olympics format is genuinely interesting as a regulatory instrument. <cite index="31-3,31-4,31-5">The conference will focus on latest developments in AI for aviation, including updates on EASA's concept paper on AI applications and ongoing rulemaking activities, with discussions on AI assurance, human factors, and ethics-based assessment, alongside presentations from industry on reinforcement learning, large language models, and knowledge-based AI technologies.</cite> <cite index="31-6">EASA is opening the conference to the best aviation industry AI cases — a novel opportunity for selected entrants to present their practices to all participants.</cite>

What EASA is really doing here is creating a structured channel for the regulator to see what the market has actually built. That's smarter than it might look from the outside. The aviation AI vendor landscape has fragmented quickly, and most of what's being developed sits somewhere between proof-of-concept and limited airline deployment — useful enough to sell, not yet well-understood enough to certify. A showcase forces vendors to articulate their systems in terms a regulator can evaluate. That friction is productive.

But here's what I keep coming back to: fifty entries, ten slots, one two-day conference. The math on this suggests a lot of interesting aviation AI is going to remain invisible to EASA's rulemaking process for another year at least. And EASA's rulemaking process matters enormously for anyone building AI that touches flight operations — because certification pathways don't exist yet for most of what the industry is trying to deploy.

## The Adoption Problem Is Upstream of the Tech

I recently polled industry professionals on the question of where AI in the cockpit should go first. The results split almost cleanly in three: 40% said maintenance and documents, 20% said pilot decision support, and 40% said AI should be kept out of the cockpit entirely. That last number is striking. Four out of ten respondents — people who work in aviation technology — aren't ready to put AI anywhere near flight operations in an active role.

That's not technophobia. That's a rational response to the absence of a credible certification framework. When you don't know how a regulator will evaluate a system, the safest answer is to not deploy it. The AI Olympics initiative is, in part, EASA's attempt to shortcut that paralysis by showing the industry that there's a pathway being built, even if the endpoint isn't fully defined yet.

From my own years working on bid processes and product delivery in this space, I've seen how much of vendor roadmap planning is driven not by what's technically possible but by what a regulator is willing to engage with. Vendors don't invest heavily in capabilities they can't eventually get approved. So the signal EASA sends by holding this showcase — that it wants to see what's being built, not just comment on proposals in the abstract — is genuinely useful for shaking investment loose in the right directions.

## What September Will Tell Us

The ten finalists who present in Cologne in September will effectively become a proxy for where the European aviation AI industry thinks it is. That's worth watching closely, because the categories of AI that make it to the stage will reveal something about what vendors believe EASA is actually ready to hear about. My working assumption is that the finalists will skew toward lower-stakes AI applications — flight data analytics, document processing, weather interpretation — rather than anything that sits directly in the decision loop on an active flight. That's not a failure of ambition; it's a reasonable read of where certification pathways currently exist.

The harder version of the question, which September probably won't answer, is how quickly EASA's ongoing rulemaking work under RMT.0742 translates into real guidance that vendors and airlines can use to design certifiable systems. <cite index="29-3">That rulemaking task is progressing in stages, with a second NPA expected in 2026 to propagate the AI trustworthiness framework into domain-specific regulations.</cite> The showcase is a useful pressure valve. The rulemaking is the actual work.

I'm genuinely curious which categories of flight-ops AI dominate the finalist list — and whether any of the ten systems presented in Cologne are from startups rather than established vendors. That ratio would tell us a lot about who EASA's evaluation criteria are actually designed for.

email_brief: EASA's AI Olympics — a new initiative tied to the EASA AI Days conference in Cologne on September 9-10, 2026 — closed for entries on July 7, two days early, after hitting its cap of 50 submissions. The top ten will present at the conference. This matters because EASA is still in the early stages of building a certification framework for aviation AI (under rulemaking task RMT.0742), and the absence of clear pathways is one of the main reasons AI adoption in flight operations has been slow despite a lot of vendor activity. The AI Olympics is worth a closer look as a regulatory instrument: it's EASA's attempt to see what the market has actually built before the rules are fully written, which is either smart regulatory learning or a useful distraction depending on your read. Today's post uses this as the anchor for a Friday opinion piece arguing that the adoption bottleneck in aviation AI is upstream of the technology itself — it's the evaluation and certification infrastructure that's lagging.
